questions.stem: The Union Budget is presented in Parliament as an Annual Financial Statement under which article of the Indian Constitution?
questions.explanation: Article 112 of the Constitution requires the President to cause to be laid before both Houses of Parliament a statement of estimated receipts and expenditure for the year — the Annual Financial Statement, commonly called the Union Budget.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Since 2017 (changed by Finance Minister Arun Jaitley), on which date is the Union Budget of India presented?
questions.explanation: The budget presentation date was advanced from the last day of February to February 1 beginning with the 2017-18 budget. This change was made to ensure that the budget is passed before the start of the financial year (April 1), allowing timely release of funds.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Fiscal Deficit is defined as:
options: Total interest payments on outstanding debt
Total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings
Capital expenditure minus capital receipts only
questions.explanation: Fiscal Deficit = Total Government Expenditure − Total Government Receipts (excluding borrowings). It represents the amount the government needs to borrow to meet its expenditures. It is the most watched deficit indicator for macroeconomic stability.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) was officially implemented across India on:
questions.explanation: GST was launched at midnight on June 30/July 1, 2017 in a special Parliament session. It replaced a complex web of central and state indirect taxes (excise duty, service tax, VAT, etc.) with a unified 'One Nation, One Tax' system.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Finance Commission of India, constituted under Article 280, performs which primary function?
options: Distributing the divisible pool of central tax revenues between the Union and States
Preparing and presenting the Union Budget
Monitoring fiscal compliance with FRBM targets
Setting GST rates for the GST Council
questions.explanation: The Finance Commission (Art 280) recommends the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Centre and States (vertical devolution) and among states (horizontal devolution). Each Finance Commission is constituted every 5 years.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 set a medium-term target of reducing fiscal deficit to what percentage of GDP?
questions.explanation: The FRBM Act (2003) aimed to achieve a revenue deficit of zero and a fiscal deficit of 3% of GDP. The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) on FRBM review also recommends a fiscal deficit of 2.5% as the long-term target with a 'debt anchor' of 60% GDP.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Primary Deficit is defined as:
options: Fiscal deficit minus interest payments on government debt
questions.explanation: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Net Interest Payments. It shows the extent to which the government needs to borrow for current year expenses (excluding inherited debt interest). A zero primary deficit means borrowings cover only past debt interest.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which constitutional authority is responsible for auditing the receipts and expenditure of the Union and State Governments to ensure legality and propriety?
options: Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG)
questions.explanation: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), established under Article 148, is the supreme audit institution of India. CAG audits all government accounts and places Audit Reports before Parliament/State Legislatures for accountability.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The GST Council, which decides GST rates and policies, is chaired by:
questions.explanation: The GST Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister. Other members include the Union Minister of State for Finance and the Finance Ministers of all States and UTs. States collectively hold 2/3 of the voting power; the Centre holds 1/3.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Planning Commission of India was dissolved in January 2015 and replaced by:
options: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India)
questions.explanation: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission in January 2015. Unlike the Planning Commission, NITI Aayog is a think tank that provides strategic policy advice; it does NOT allocate funds to States and Ministries.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of the following is a DIRECT tax in India?
questions.explanation: Income tax (both personal income tax and corporate income tax/CIT) is a direct tax — it is paid directly by the person or entity on whom it is imposed. GST, Customs Duty, and Excise Duty are indirect taxes (levied on goods/services and passed on to the consumer).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Capital receipts of the Central Government include which of the following?
options: Income tax and corporate tax collected
Interest earned on government loans to states
Market borrowings (G-Sec issuance) and disinvestment proceeds
questions.explanation: Capital receipts include market borrowings (government securities), disinvestment proceeds, recovery of loans, and external borrowings — these either create a liability or reduce an asset. Tax revenue and non-tax revenue (interest, dividends) are Revenue Receipts.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which budget year saw the removal of the distinction between 'Plan expenditure' and 'Non-Plan expenditure' in the Indian Union Budget?
questions.explanation: The Plan/Non-Plan distinction was abolished from the Union Budget 2017-18, on the recommendation of the C. Rangarajan committee. The expenditure is now classified as 'Capital Expenditure' and 'Revenue Expenditure', which is economically more meaningful.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 15th Finance Commission (covering 2021-26), chaired by N.K. Singh, recommended that States receive what share of the divisible pool of central taxes?
questions.explanation: The 15th Finance Commission recommended a 41% share of the divisible pool for States (slightly reduced from the 14th FC's 42% due to Jammu & Kashmir becoming a UT, thereby reducing the state count needing central transfers).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In India's GST four-tier rate structure, which rate is applied to luxury goods, demerit goods (tobacco, aerated drinks), and high-end automobiles?
questions.explanation: The highest GST slab is 28%, applied to luxury items (five-star hotel stays, premium cars), demerit/sin goods (tobacco, pan masala, aerated drinks). An additional cess is levied on top of 28% GST for certain items to fund the Compensation Cess to states.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget) is presented to Parliament by:
options: Prime Minister on behalf of the Union Cabinet
President of India in a joint sitting
Union Finance Minister on the floor of the Lok Sabha
Lok Sabha Speaker at the commencement of the budget session
questions.explanation: The Union Finance Minister presents the Budget in the Lok Sabha on the appointed date. The Economic Survey (reviewing the economy) is traditionally presented the day before the Budget.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Revenue Deficit occurs when:
options: Total borrowings exceed tax revenues collected
Fiscal deficit becomes larger than the primary deficit
questions.explanation: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts. A positive revenue deficit means the government is borrowing to meet its day-to-day (non-asset creating) expenses, which is considered fiscally unsound since it does not add to national assets.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB) is a budgeting approach that requires:
options: All expenses to be justified from scratch each budget period (not just incremental changes from the previous year)
The budget deficit must be zero
Both revenue and capital budgets must be balanced
Only capital expenditure is planned; revenue expenditure is automatic
questions.explanation: In Zero-Based Budgeting, every function and department starts from a 'zero base' each year — all expenditure proposals must be re-justified on cost-benefit grounds, regardless of previous year spending. Traditional budgeting only looks at incremental changes.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: GST was introduced in India to replace multiple indirect taxes, with the key objective of creating:
options: A more progressive direct tax system
One Nation, One Tax (unified indirect tax across India)
A uniform direct tax code replacing income tax
A Central government-controlled integrated tax system
questions.explanation: The core objective of GST was 'One Nation, One Tax' — replacing the fragmented indirect tax structure (central excise, service tax, state VAT, entry tax, etc.) with a single, integrated tax, eliminating the cascading effect ('tax on tax') and creating a common national market.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Gender Budgeting — the practice of applying a gender lens to budgetary allocations — was first introduced in India's Union Budget in:
questions.explanation: Gender Budgeting was introduced in the Union Budget 2005-06. It involves a Gender Budget Statement that shows the proportion of spending on women and girls across government departments, promoting gender-responsive fiscal policy.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included in the Central Government's revenue receipts?
options: Income tax collected by the Central government
GST component flowing to the Centre (CGST)
questions.explanation: Market borrowings (issuance of G-Secs/T-Bills) are Capital Receipts, not Revenue Receipts. Revenue receipts include tax revenue (income tax, corporate tax, CGST, customs) and non-tax revenue (interest receipts, dividends from PSUs, fees). Borrowings create liabilities.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Under the GST framework, which body serves as the forum where the Centre and States jointly decide on GST rates, exemptions, and policy issues?
questions.explanation: The GST Council (Article 279A) is the constitutional body where the Centre and all 36 States/UTs jointly decide on all GST-related matters — rates, exemptions, threshold limits, etc. Decisions require a 75% supermajority weighted vote.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Union Budget consists of two main parts. What are they?
options: Revenue Budget (revenue receipts and expenditure) and Capital Budget (capital receipts and expenditure)
Defence Budget and Civil Administration Budget
questions.explanation: The Union Budget is divided into: (1) Revenue Budget — showing revenue receipts (taxes, non-tax) and revenue expenditure (salaries, subsidies, interest payments); and (2) Capital Budget — showing capital receipts (borrowings, disinvestment) and capital expenditure (infrastructure, loans to states).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: India's financial year runs from:
questions.explanation: India's financial/fiscal year runs from April 1 to March 31. This was set historically during British rule to align with the UK financial year (which used to be April–March). The government's budget, accounting, and annual reports follow this cycle.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Appropriation Bill, presented as part of the Union Budget, gives the government the authority to:
options: Levy and collect taxes for the year
Borrow money from the Reserve Bank of India
Withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund of India for approved expenditure
Amend tax rates under the Finance Bill
questions.explanation: The Appropriation Bill authorizes the government to withdraw funds from the Consolidated Fund of India (CFA) to meet expenditures approved by Parliament. No money can be taken from the CFA except under an Appropriation Act. The Finance Bill, on the other hand, covers tax proposals.
questions.subject: Economics
